title: Enhancing Undergraduate Literacy in STEM Contexts: A Systematic Literature Review of Interventions
abstract: Abstract Despite the increased importance of literacy for STEM professionals, current instruction often fails to properly prepare students for careers. STEM degree programs are often already full of content-specific requirements, making it essential to identify effective ways to integrate literacy instruction within existing curricula. The purpose of this study is to systematically review published research investigating strategies for developing undergraduate students’ STEM literacy skills to discover what we already know as a field and evaluate how literacy-focused interventions can support student achievement. We screened over 2,000 articles and included 85 in the present review. Our findings demonstrate that substantial research has been conducted in developing literacy in STEM contexts, especially with students attending four-year institutions and in life science fields. Our results suggest that short, targeted interventions can effectively improve discrete literacy skills, particularly when paired with explicit instruction.

title: Navigating the Academic Tower: Faculty Perceptions of Counteroffers in Higher Education
abstract: Abstract While counteroffers are a key component of faculty retention, limited research explores how faculty perceive and experience these negotiations and how this might impact institutional departure. Using Quantitative Ethnography and Epistemic Network Analysis, this study analyzes qualitative responses from faculty who completed the COACHE Faculty Retention and Exit Study to examine how they describe their counteroffer process and whether their experiences differ based on demographic factors (e.g., race and gender) and professional characteristics (e.g., rank, academic area, and departure status). Findings reveal that faculty frequently interpreted counteroffers as signals of institutional value–or lack thereof–with themes of dismissiveness, procedural opacity, and inconsistent treatment emerging across personal and professional identities. Notably, Asian or Asian American faculty showed strong co-occurrences between institutional ambiguity and feelings of dismissal, and their network was statistically significant from that of Black or African American faculty. Leveraging the Untapped Potential of Research Conversations
abstract: Abstract Students participate in research conversations for complex reasons including the desire to advance knowledge and influence policy about issues that matter to them. Further, the opportunity to feel seen and heard is a benefit students receive from being asked to articulate their thoughts and feelings. In this article, we explore our experiences as qualitative researchers whose participants guided them into this new terrain of participant motivation. We found feedback provided during member-checking, advocacy, and opportunities for reflection to be the primary ways students experienced value in being research participants. We identify the implications of our findings about participants’ motivations and situate them within the context of our experiences navigating higher education institutions driven by industrial logic. We offer recommendations grounded in these experiences and the related interdisciplinary scholarship.

Evolution and Transformation of Higher Education Internationalization: Clusters and Innovative Paradigms
abstract: Abstract The internationalization of higher education has evolved from mobility-centered strategies toward more complex frameworks that integrate intercultural, pedagogical, and ethical dimensions. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of 1,790 scientific publications indexed in Scopus between 1972 and 2025 to map the evolution, thematic density, and emerging paradigms of the field. The analysis examines research production and new trends in higher education internationalization to identify influential concepts, nodes, and clusters shaping contemporary debates. Results reveal an exponential increase in scientific production since the 2000s, accompanied by a shift from descriptive approaches—focused on cooperation and mobility—to multidimensional perspectives emphasizing intercultural competence, internationalization of the curriculum, global citizenship, sustainability, and educational innovation. Nine thematic clusters were identified, spanning areas such as governance and policy, pedagogical transformation, linguistic diversity, social justice, strategic management, and transnational education. title: The Contributions–Impact Model of Faculty Burnout: A Conceptual Framework for Higher Education
A Multilevel Approach to Examining Transfer Student Belonging in Different Academic Majors
abstract: Abstract As the number of transfer students at four-year institutions continues to grow, questions remain about how their experiences vary once they arrive at four-year institutions. While previous research has documented the academic and social challenges transfer students face, less is known about how a student’s academic major shapes their transition, particularly their sense of belonging to the institution. This study explores how sense of belonging differs between transfer students and non-transfer students and whether this difference varies across majors. Using multilevel modeling and institutional survey data from graduating seniors, we found that transfer students reported lower levels of belonging than their non-transfer peers, though this effect varied across majors. Although differences in sense of belonging across majors were modest, some programs exhibited larger gaps between transfer and non-transfer students. These findings contribute to efforts to better understand how academic programs shape student experience and highlight the continued importance of supporting transfer student integration.

The Default College: How Racialized Messages Impact Black Student Perceptions of HBCUs and PWIs
abstract: Abstract This study used interviews with 20 Black graduate and undergraduate students, Critical Race Theory, and Calmore's Racialized Space Framework to investigate how historical and societal racial narratives shape the messages Black students receive about HBCUs and PWIs. It also explores how later experiences with these institutions impact students' pre-existing beliefs. Four notable findings emerge: (1) Black students often receive racialized and oppositional messages about HBCUs and PWIs that influence how they perceive these institutions and what they consider the ideal college experience; (2) these messages are particularly powerful when Black students have limited firsthand knowledge of these institutions. title: Just Innovation Is Not Enough: A Multi-Level Framework for Institutionalising Teaching and Learning Innovations in Higher Education
abstract: Abstract Despite decades of interest in teaching and learning (T&L) innovations, many fail to become institutionalised. This paper addresses this persistent challenge by proposing a new conceptual model—the Innovation Institutionalisation Framework (IIF). Developed through an abductive synthesis of institutional theory constructs—namely, DiMaggio and Powell’s (1983) framework of macro-level isomorphic pressures and Cartel et al.’s (2019) framework of micro-level institutional work—the IIF offers a dynamic, theoretically coherent, and practically relevant perspective on how structural forces and agentic efforts can be aligned to facilitate the institutionalisation of innovative educational solutions. The IIF contributes to theory, policy, and the practice of individual innovators. Theoretically, it bridges macro- and micro-level analyses, extending the institutional theory toolkit in higher education research and offering a more integrated account of institutionalisation processes. It moves beyond approaches that treat these levels in isolation by conceptualising institutionalisation as a process of mutual reinforcement between system-level arrangements and localised action. title: “There are no Footsteps to Follow”: A Qualitative Study Exploring Intersectional Experiences of Contemporary Students Navigating Public Higher Education
abstract: Abstract Despite attempts to equalize access to U.S. higher education for contemporary students from historically marginalized groups, structural obstacles persist within universities, particularly among students struggling to meet their basic needs. To understand how interlocking power relations (e.g., racism, classism) in systems of higher education impact contemporary students, we conducted a qualitative analysis of 11 focus groups with 58 students who utilized basic needs services across five University of California campuses. We identified three themes that characterize the experiences of contemporary students who are at intersectional positions (e.g., low-income, first generation to attend college): (1) they continue to face challenges navigating a system designed for traditional students; (2) students are challenged by the lack of access to the power and privilege that operate in student-related institutional operations and policies; and (3) university personnel’s lack of structural competency creates additional burdens for students. title: “What Was College Made For?” Exploring College Students’ Civic Engagement Outcomes by College Major
abstract: Abstract In light of political discourse around return-on-investment (ROI) of obtaining postsecondary degrees, one often overlooked outcome of a college education is students’ development of their civic engagement. We were concerned about whether specific degree programs targeted for elimination may enroll students with higher levels of civic engagement. We used the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009 (HSLS:09) from the National Council of Educational Statistics (NCES) to examine differences across academic major categories in several measures of civic engagement including 1) registered to vote in the U.S., 2) engagement in community service/volunteer work, 3) perceived importance of contributing to society, and 4) participating in a community-based project for a college course. Employing multinomial propensity score estimation, we found meaningful differences across majors in civic engagement. College majors often perceived as lower on ROI had higher levels of civic engagement on most measures. title: A Positioning Analysis of School-to-Work Transitions: Narratives of Chinese Master’s STEM Students in the U.S
abstract: Abstract School-to-work transitions have primarily been examined through structural and economic lenses, focusing on factors such as labor market demands, skill alignment, and employment outcomes. However, the nuanced personal and relational dimensions of these transitions remain underexplored, particularly for international master’s students in STEM fields. Drawing on Bamberg’s (2020) positioning theory, this paper analyzes the narratives of Chinese master’s STEM students in the U.S. to illuminate how their identities, aspirations, and challenges are dynamically constructed and negotiated during this pivotal phase. The findings reveal how participants position themselves reflexively and interactively in relation to dominant cultural and professional expectations, negotiating key dilemmas such as sameness versus difference, agency versus passivity, and continuity versus change. These narratives further demonstrate the interplay of relationality, temporality, and self-formation in shaping the transition process. This study argues that applying a positioning lens deepens our understanding of school-to-work transitions and concludes with implications for future research in this area.

Strategists, Contrarians, Enthusiasts, and Advocates: A Q Methodology Study of Views on Institutional Accreditation
abstract: Abstract Despite the importance of accreditation in U.S. higher education, scholarship examining faculty and administrators’ perspectives on it is limited, anecdotal, or institution specific. This Q methodology study investigates the subjective views of 54 faculty and administrators engaged in institutional accreditation work across the United States. Q methodology enables researchers to blend quantitative and qualitative approaches to reveal distinct and empirically grounded perspectives on important phenomena. We identified four perspectives on accreditation. Standards Strategists assert accreditation is clear and fair but disconnected from academic quality. Cost-Conscious Contrarians view accreditation as accountability that sacrifices autonomy. Effectiveness Enthusiasts believe accreditation promotes improvement but question its requirements, processes, and external value. Accreditation Advocates see its potential for institutions that devote significant time and energy to engaging in the process. “D.E.I. Is Not Working on College Campuses”: An Analysis of Liberal Opinions on DEI Initiatives
abstract: Abstract As the Trump administration, MAGA-aligned actors, and right-wing organizations increasingly frame diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) as a catchall term for failing progressive initiatives, assessing liberal perspectives on DEI becomes critical, particularly in higher education where DEI programs face mounting political pressure. Grounded in institutional theory, Critical Race Theory and Critical Whiteness Studies, this paper moves beyond the partisan culture war binary to analyze fracturing liberal support for DEI. Methodologically, it uses Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) to examine how readers of the New York Times ( The Times ) debated DEI’s goals and implementation in response to an August 2024 opinion piece on college DEI. Treating reader comments as a liberal-coded discursive site linked to higher education’s cultural legitimacy, the analysis reveals ambivalent liberal support for DEI. While 13% of commenters support DEI goals and implementation and 34% oppose both, a 53% majority supports DEI aims while critiquing its effectiveness, implementation, perceived dogmatism, and ideological homogeneity. title: The Other Half: Understanding How High School Practitioners Help Implement a Community College Dual Credit Policy
abstract: Abstract In summer 2023, Texas launched the FAST initiative to fund free dual credit courses for high school students eligible for free or reduced-price lunch. Drawing on a sensemaking framework, this qualitative case study examined how ten high school dual-credit practitioners in one Texas metropolitan area understood and implemented the policy during its first year. Findings indicate that while community colleges and leaders supported implementation, high school staff faced communication challenges due to limited capacity and training. Despite these barriers, practitioners used different strategies to raise awareness among students and families. The study highlights both the promise of the FAST initiative and the on-the-ground complexities of implementing a policy to expand access to college in high school settings, offering a real-time account of policy implementation and extending sensemaking theory to cross-sector settings that characterize dual-credit policies.

Enhancing Visual Literacy Competency in Arts Students Through Creative Visual Thinking: A Mixed-Methods Case Study
abstract: Abstract Visual literacy (VL) is a fundamental competency for arts students; nevertheless, its rigorous evaluation is a challenge due to the subjective nature of visual interpretation and the intricate interplay between visual and verbal competencies. Using the Common European Framework of Reference for Visual Literacy (CEFR-VL) to address this challenge, students identified a significant issue: the random distribution of the 16 subcompetencies in the original CEFR-VL visual model and the consequent difficulty in comprehending those subcompetencies. This mixed-methods case study reports on a trial performed to first examine how visual thinking activities during a series of diagram sketching sessions affected students’ abilities to recustomize the CEFR-VL visual model. Second, it explores how the revised CEFR-VL visual model improved the performance of arts students in achieving CEFR-VL subcompetencies and assists educators with their assessments. Initially, the students collectively restructured the CEFR‑VL model by recategorizing its subcompetencies into four functional channels through diagram sketching activities and guided inquiry. Family-Supportive Supervisor Behavior and Flexibility Stigma among Tenure-track Faculty
abstract: Abstract Although many universities have policies that pause/extend the pre-tenure probationary period when a faculty member’s family adds new children, many faculty members do not choose to use such policies. Drawing from the organizational science literature on family-friendly policies and supports, we propose that such choices may be affected by a perceived ‘flexibility stigma.’ We hypothesize that department / unit chairs’ engagement in family-supportive supervisor behavior (FSSB) relates to lower perceived stigma, which in turn relates to intent to use the policy. Furthermore, we hypothesize that this effect is moderated by gender, as well as whether one is in a position to potentially utilize the policy (i.e., pre-tenure vs. post-tenure). Using a sample of 136 tenured or tenure-track faculty, we examined both individual-level and shared (department-level) perceptions of FSSB, the perceived stigma associated with extending the probationary period for tenure (e.g., pausing the “tenure clock”), and hesitancy to use such a policy. title: Reframing Value in Higher Education: Individual Pricing Data and the Transparency Gap
abstract: Abstract The study examines existing weaknesses in assessing the economic value of higher education from the perspective of the consumer, rooted in the lack of individualized pricing data. Despite decades of policy efforts aimed at improving tuition transparency, students and researchers remain constrained by publicly available institutional averages and opaque pricing structures that obscure the actual costs paid by individual students. To address this problem, a novel dataset is introduced comprising crowdsourced financial aid award letters and student demographic information, offering a rare and actionable view into real college prices. The paper offers an overview of the historical and conceptual underpinnings of tuition opacity; critiques the limitations in existing public data sources; and presents illustrative empirical insights from a case study of four universities within a single state. By comparing publicly reported prices with actual prices paid, findings reveal that publicly reported pricing metrics often misrepresent the true costs students face, with significant implications for equity, access, and decision-making. title: Young Adults’ Public and Private Support for Higher Education in America
abstract: Abstract Given recent media attention and political narratives questioning the value of higher education, we survey young Americans about their attitudes towards college. We explore two dimensions of attitudes towards college – higher education as a private good and as a public good. We find most young people still believe most of their peers should go to college, and most want their children to go to college, although there are meaningful differences across demographic groups and different student experiences, with practical and political implications. We find evidence suggesting that exposure to higher education and providing students with adequate information during their own college search process may be meaningful predictors of young adults’ attitudes about college.

title: Labor for Learning: Financial Structure and Institutional Characteristics of Work Colleges
abstract: Abstract This study documents the financial characteristics of all ten federally designated work colleges using a decade of institutional data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (2014–2023). Work colleges are a small group of private, nonprofit institutions that require all residential students to participate in structured, compensated labor programs as a condition of enrollment, with the explicit goal of reducing reliance on tuition revenue. Using distributional benchmarks, longitudinal financial trajectories, institution-level profiles, and a lasso-selected logistic classification model, I characterize the financial distinctiveness of work colleges relative to approximately 1,600 comparable private, nonprofit, four-year institutions. Work colleges rely far less on tuition revenue (median tuition share of 25 percent versus 56 percent for comparators), draw substantially more from private gifts, and carry lower average federal loan burdens than peers. While work college institutional profiles vary, they maintain operating margins and net financial positions that are broadly comparable to, and in some cases stronger than, those of similar institutions. title: Reconceptualising University Governance as Social Relations Work: Purpose, Orientation, and Practice in an Integrated Framework
abstract: Abstract South African public universities face converging pressures that compliance-based, managerial, and structural approaches to governance cannot meet. Historical redress, ideological contestation, global anti-DEI currents, and the legacies of cooperative governance arrangements that too often operate symbolically have exposed the limits of prevailing frameworks. This paper advances a conceptual contribution to governance theory by integrating three frameworks: Heracleous and Lan’s (2022) “Third Possibility,” which reframes the purpose of governance as stewardship grounded in socioemotional wealth, long-term legacy, and societal embeddedness; Complexity Theory, which supplies the orientation through which universities are understood as complex adaptive systems requiring adaptive rather than controlling governance; and the King V Code of Corporate Governance in South Africa, which provides the practice architecture through its apply-and-explain regime and outcomes-based logic. Beyond Individual Social Mobility: Black and Latine Students Envisioning Liberatory Purposes of Community College
abstract: Abstract Discussions on the purposes of higher education remain focused on the university despite the heterogeneity of sectors, which limits a richer understanding from various perspectives (Ashwin, 2022). Students’ perspectives also remain underexplored (Cuellar et al., 2022). Informed neoliberalism’s impact on higher education (Mintz, 2021) as well as critical race theory in education (Solorzano, 1998) we consider how community college students articulate the purposes of higher education through their experiences based on interviews with 18 Latine and 25 Black community college students. Findings indicated that neoliberal ideology informed students’ views of higher education more broadly. Simultaneously, findings challenged neoliberal ideologies by highlighting that participants engaged in a liberatory ideology to maintain a vision of higher education that centered families and collectivist benefits. Participants viewed the purpose of college as an opportunity to support their Latine and Black communities. Perceptions of College Advising Corps Advisors: Their Experiences and Values
abstract: Abstract The College Advising Corps (CAC) is an innovative program that places college admission advisors in high schools to assist underrepresented students. This case study explored how 11 participants constructed their own experience of working as a CAC advisor. The findings resulted in five major themes including Advisor Experience, Advisor Roles, Rewards of CAC Work, Recognition of Strengths, and Personal and Professional Growth. Describing their experiences as overwhelmingly positive and rewarding, the advisors emphasized the importance of relationships they develop with students and discussed attributes, such as cultural awareness, needed for the job. Yet, they conceded struggles related to the impact of COVID and workload, with increased challenges for those participants working as the sole advisor on a school campus. Having at least two advisors on each campus may allow for a more beneficial experience, both for the advisors and the students they serve. The advisors benefitted from their experience through an increased sense of confidence in their abilities, as well as fulfilment in giving back to others.
